Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00449

This does not contradict the experience the mystics describe, in which they lose awareness of themselves. It happens when a person stops attending to themselves and turns wholly toward God. Yet a created being’s separate identity still stands between it and God like a veil. That veil continues to limit what can be seen. Even if the person no longer notices their separate identity while contemplating God, its effect remains. As al-Ḥallāj says:
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00450
Between You and me, my “I” keeps coming between us. By Your grace, remove my “I” from between us.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00451
The Throne Section
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00452

Know, seeker of truth—may God strengthen you with His spirit—that knowledge, like ignorance, has two forms: simple and self-aware. In the simple form, you grasp something without noticing that you have grasped it or recognising what it is. In the self-aware form, you grasp the thing and also know that you have grasped it and what it is.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00453

With this distinction in place, we can say that simple knowledge of God is present in every person's original nature. Once we have understood what knowing is and set aside what does not belong to it, what we know directly in any thing is a way in which that thing exists. This holds whether we know through the senses, imagination, or reason, and whether the thing is present to us or known through a representation.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00454

Mystics who have reached this knowledge, along with philosophers who know God, have established that each thing exists through a particular reality of its own, connected to the existence of God, the Living One who needs nothing else to sustain Him. What makes it true to say that things exist is their own real identities, each connected to divine existence. We will prove that these existing identities are levels of God's self-disclosure, and flashes of His majesty and beauty. So to know any thing is to see it in the way it is connected to the Necessary Being—through the very existence by which it is real. This can happen only through awareness of God's own reality, because His reality itself is the end of the chain of possible things and the goal of every dependence. It is not through some other aspect of Him: all His aspects and attributes return to His own reality, as we will explain in its proper place, God willing.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00455

Whoever knows anything, in any way, has therefore known God, even if unaware of that knowledge. Only God's closest friends recognise what is happening. It is related that ʿAlī said: “I never saw anything without seeing God before it.” Another version says “with it” or “in it”; all are true. This unreflective awareness of God is therefore present in every servant. It does not mean that anyone fully comprehends God's reality, which reason has already shown to be impossible.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00456

Self-aware knowledge of God, by contrast, is not given to everyone. It may come through direct spiritual witnessing, as it does for the most devoted mystics, or through reasoning about God's attributes and works, as it does for thoughtful people. This second kind of knowledge is what makes religious duty and the message of the prophets meaningful. Here a person may be right or wrong; here too belong judgments of faith and unbelief and differences in people's spiritual standing. The first, simple kind is never touched by error or ignorance. As the Persian poet says: “Knowledge of the Real is innate in every being; knowing that one knows is the work of thought.”
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00457

We can now see that everything perceived by the five senses, or by any other power of perception, is a manifestation of the divine reality. He is the first Beloved and the highest goal of human life. A person sees Him through the eyes, but not in the sense taught by the Ashʿarite theologians; hears His words through the ears; smells His fragrance through the nose; and feels His touch through the skin, but not as those who give God a body imagine. Exalted is He above that. In this way, we perceive the true Beloved through all our powers and bodily organs. Yet He is beyond place and direction, and His reality is free of matter and bodily form.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00458

This is what those who have reached direct spiritual vision agree upon. They are the finest of God's servants. In the sense just described, all beings are aware: they know their Lord, praise Him, witness His beauty, and hear His speech. This is what the Qur'an points to when it says: “There is nothing that does not glorify Him with praise, though you do not understand their praise.” Praise and the recognition of God's holiness are impossible without knowing Him.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00459

God's saying, “When He wills something, His command is only to say to it, ‘Be,’ and it is,” clearly shows that all beings understand their Lord, know their Creator, and hear His speech. For carrying out a command follows from hearing it and understanding what is intended, each according to the listener's capacity and the way the listener perceives. God's saying to the heavens and the earth, “Come, willingly or unwillingly,” and their reply, “We come willingly,” makes the same point.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00460
An objection and its answer
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00461

You may say that existence is a single kind of thing, since its meaning is one and shared by all. A kind has the same necessary features in every individual: whatever belongs to one must belong to the others, since what follows from a thing's nature cannot fail to follow from it. So if existence requires that something be in a subject—or requires that it not be in a subject—the same must be true of both the Necessary and the possible. If existence requires neither, then the Necessary Being needs some outside cause to make Him necessary.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00462

The familiar reply is to deny that existence is a single kind that applies in exactly the same way to everything. A shared concept does not require that the things it describes have the same reality. One concept can apply to things whose realities differ. So particular existences may differ in reality: the Necessary Being's existence can be free of matter, while other existences are joined to it, even though the general concept “existence” applies to them all. The concept might apply uniformly, as “essence” does to different essences and “individuality” to different individuals. Or it might apply by degrees, as “light” does to sunlight and other lights. Sunlight lets a person with night blindness see, while other lights do not. A single concept of existence therefore does not prove that every particular existence has the same reality and the same necessary features. We have already seen that existence applies by degrees, and that it is earlier, more basic, and stronger in the Necessary Being than in possible things.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00463

Yet this usual reply is unsound as it stands. The things to which we apply the concept of existence are not separate kinds of reality. Existence is one reality. It is not shared as a universal nature is shared by its members, whether that nature belongs to their essence or is an added feature. Universality and particularity belong to possible essences. Existence, as we have seen, is neither universal nor particular; each instance is particular through its own concrete reality and needs no further feature to make it so. Nor does its being existent require another existence, because its existence is its very reality.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00464

As we will explain when we discuss degrees of existence, one reality can differ in its levels and expressions through that very reality, without anything being added to it. Thus existence itself accounts for what makes each thing distinct, for what comes first and what comes later, for necessity and possibility, for what exists independently and what exists in another, and for completeness and deficiency.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00465

These features belong to existence itself, though recognising this takes a keen mind and a sensitive understanding. It is surprising that al-Khaṭīb al-Rāzī insists on only two possibilities: either the word “existence” has different meanings in different cases, or every existing thing must have the same necessary features. He seems not to distinguish between sharing a meaning and sharing the same reality. More astonishing still, in some of his books he says that existence applies by degrees, yet insists on his objection as if it could not be questioned. He has not distinguished agreement in meaning from agreement in reality and essence.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00466

Others reason as follows. If existence is added to essence, that is what they set out to prove. If it is not added, they say, a concept that applies uniformly cannot describe something as a feature of another thing in one case but not in another. And if the concept applies by degrees, existence must be a feature of everything. Neither argument works.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00467

Even a concept that applies uniformly need not belong essentially to everything it describes. It can apply to existences that differ in whether they are features of something else. And the conclusion we need—that particular existence is added to reality—does not follow. One thing described by the abstract concept “existence” could be a self-subsisting, independent reality, fundamentally different from the other particular existences that have essences. This is especially clear on our view: existence is the primary reality, while other existences are manifestations of God's face and beauty, rays of His light and perfection, and shadows of His majesty and power.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00468
The second claim is also unsound. It assumes that a concept applied by degrees must be outside the realities of its individuals and their levels. We will return to this point, God willing.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00469
Chapter — The Necessary Being is necessary in every respect
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00470

The point of this chapter is that the Necessary Being has no aspect of possibility. Whatever can be attributed to Him as possible in the broadest sense is in fact necessary for Him. One consequence is that no perfection remains for Him to acquire. But this consequence is not the same as the principle itself, as many have assumed. Being necessary in every respect belongs to the Necessary Being alone; having no perfection left to acquire does not. Immaterial beings of light also have nothing left to acquire. If one of them could still gain a perfection, it would have the capacity to receive change. That would subject it to motion and the conditions of physical bodies. It would then be bodily and darkened, despite being immaterial and luminous—a contradiction.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00471

There are two proofs of the principle. The first is the proof I have laboured to establish. If God, considered in Himself, could either have or lack some perfection, His reality would be made up of parts. The next chapter will show why that is impossible. He must therefore possess the perfection necessarily, not merely as a possibility.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00472

Here is the second proof. Suppose God's own reality were not enough to account for all His attributes. At least one attribute would then come to Him from something else. The presence of that other thing would cause the attribute to be present, and its absence would cause the attribute to be absent. For when a cause exists, its effect follows; when the cause is absent, so is its effect.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00473

If this were so, God's reality, considered just as it is and without any condition, would not make His existence necessary. His existence would be necessary only with the attribute present or only with it absent. If it were necessary with the attribute present, then the attribute would not really come from something else: it would belong to God's reality just as it is, without taking the other thing into account. And if necessity applied only on the condition that the attribute was present, then God's necessity would not be essential and eternal. But if His existence were necessary with the attribute absent, then the attribute's absence would not be caused by the absence of its cause. And if His necessity depended on that absence, it would not be essential and eternal either. Far above this is God. If His existence is not necessary without a condition, He is not necessary in Himself.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00474
A clarification and a stronger formulation
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00475

A familiar objection runs like this. At most, the proof shows that an attribute's presence or absence depends on something else. It does not show that God's own reality depends on that thing. What does it mean to consider God's reality without the other thing? If it means simply not thinking about that thing, the argument fails: overlooking something does not make it absent. If it means that the thing really is absent, the reasoning goes through, but its conclusion is no contradiction. On that assumption, considering God's reality without the supposed conditions would itself be impossible. An impossible assumption may lead to another impossibility.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00476

The proof is stronger if we put it this way. Consider God's reality just as it is, without bringing the other thing into the account, whether present or absent. God's existence would then have to be necessary either with the attribute or without it. Neither alternative works. We cannot consider an effect as existing while leaving its cause out of account. Nor can we consider the attribute absent while leaving out the cause of its absence. In reality, God's necessary existence must fall into one of these two cases. So if we consider His reality without the relevant condition, His necessity itself becomes impossible. He must therefore be considered with that condition, and His necessity would depend on something else. The conclusion follows, while it is clear that the Necessary Being cannot depend on another.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00477

Someone might say that setting aside a cause in thought, whether it exists or not, does not mean that the cause is absent in reality. So the effect could still be present or absent, caused in reality, and we would have no contradiction. After all, considering an essence just as it is does not mean that we consider it without whatever existence or nonexistence happens to accompany it in reality. The essence remains one way or the other.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00478

We answer: an essence can be considered at a level apart from reality. At that level, it is not a container for either real existence or real nonexistence. Nothing belongs to it there except itself and what follows from its own nature, whether by way of affirmation or denial. It has no real relation to other things, whether they exist or not. So reason can consider an essence without considering anything else, even when something else accompanies it in reality.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00479

Existence is different. It is reality itself, fully actual. There is no separate level at which we can consider it apart from what exists or does not exist. It is the source of existing things and what makes their reality possible. Where existence is present, absence and nonexistence are overcome. At its own level, existence is either at the same level as another reality—as with God's perfections, which exist at the same level as His own reality—or it is a level of absence, where existence falls short. That deficiency is far beneath the Necessary Being and comes after Him by many degrees. The stages of possibility and dependence arise through successive steps away from complete existence, which is free of all need.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00480

So any attribute we suppose God to have, when considered together with His reality, is either present or absent. In either case, its cause must be considered along with it. Just as the existence or nonexistence of an effect follows from the existence or nonexistence of its cause, our understanding and consideration of an effect follow from our understanding and consideration of its cause. This is the strongest way anyone can argue the point.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00481

One might object that this proof also applies to the relations and connections that belong to God. It would mean that all these relations were necessary to Him in His own reality, without any other thing contributing to them, and that they could never arise or change. But God's reality is not enough for these relations, since they depend on many different things that come and go. Avicenna accepts this in The Healing: “We do not mind considering God's essence together with a relation that is possible in itself. For God is not necessary in Himself insofar as He is the cause of Zayd; He is necessary in Himself because He is what He is.”
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00482

Those whose hearts are lit by the light of transcendent wisdom do not accept this answer. Many of Avicenna's followers have repeated it, including the author of The Commentary on the Abstract, who says that the Necessary Being can be possible in relation to another, and that another can be possible in relation to Him, even though God cannot be possible in Himself or through something else.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00483

They have missed this: the Necessary Being is necessary not only in Himself but also in relation to the possible things that depend on Him. Those things, too, are necessarily present in relation to Him, because their existence is inseparable from what He gives them. Their view might make sense if there were another Necessary Being, with other possible things depending on that second source. But there is no such source.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00484

The existence of things is necessary through Him, since He brings them into being and makes them necessary through their cause. Just as they are necessary through the cause that brings them forth, they are necessary in relation to that cause—and the cause is necessary in relation to them. To be necessary in relation to another means that the thing must exist in view of that other. The other cannot but make it necessary, whether through its own active outpouring or through the dependent thing's inherent need and appeal for support. A possible being is possible in itself, but necessary through its complete cause. This necessity belongs to it either because of its own dependent nature, or because its source brings it forth and sustains it.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00485

The truth is that God's relations to possible things, His role as their Creator and Sustainer, and His light reaching things that can exist are not later than those possible essences. His relation to them is not like ordinary relations between things, which come after the things related. The basis of His relational attributes is His own reality: His reality itself is enough for the mind to recognise these relations and what they relate to.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00486

Just as God's complete, unified knowledge takes in all things and their relations to Him, and His perfect power brings all things into being, so too His own reality is enough for us to understand every relation, how it attaches, and what it connects. In the divine realm there is none of the negative states found among creatures: nonexistence, possibility, uncertainty, play, coming-to-be, passing away, change, transience, or dependence.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00487

It is astonishing that Avicenna, with all his learning, insight, and intelligence, did not grasp this point. More astonishing still, he understood it elsewhere. In his Annotations, he says that all things are necessary in relation to the First Being, and that there is no possibility there at all. The book called Theology, attributed to the First Teacher, also clearly states that all possible things are present to the First Source with necessity and certainty.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00488

What appears to us as things coming to be, following one another, and changing does so in relation to certain levels of existence. A thing's disappearance from one level does not mean that it has disappeared from every other level—how much less from the reality of existence, which encompasses all things and preserves every level and mode of being? We will explain this further, God willing.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00489
Chapter — The Necessary Being is one, not merely a kind confined to a single individual
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00490

We have seen that existence is not one member of some broader kind. And although the Necessary Being is distinct through His very reality, that fact alone does not prove that there cannot be another Necessary Being. Some have argued that if a thing is distinct through its very reality, there can be only one member of its kind. But that is not enough to establish God's oneness. We can still imagine several different realities, each necessary in itself and each distinct through its own reality. We therefore need another proof.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00491

Suppose there were two Necessary Beings. We would call both “necessary in existence,” yet their realities would have to differ. What made one different from the other would have to be its whole reality, part of its reality, or something outside its reality.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00492

If the difference were the whole reality of one, then the shared necessity of existence would lie outside that being's reality. This is impossible, since necessity of existence is the very reality of the Necessary Being. If the difference were part of its reality, it would be composite. A composite depends on its parts, and anything that depends on something else is possible, not necessary. If the difference were something outside its reality, then the Necessary Being would depend on something else to be particular. Any feature added to a thing and distinct from its reality needs a cause. That cause would have to be either the Necessary Being itself or something else. If it were the Necessary Being itself, the cause would have to be particular before its effect was particular, so the Necessary Being would have to precede itself. If the cause were something else, the Necessary Being would depend on it for its very existence, since particularity is either identical with existence or at the same level as existence. Dependence in existence is incompatible with being necessary in itself.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00493

Someone may object that saying “necessity of existence is the reality of the Necessary Being” does not mean that this reality is identical to the feature of necessity. It may mean only that this reality naturally gives rise to the feature. Then two beings could share necessity of existence as a feature while differing in their complete realities.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00494

We answer that the philosophers mean that the Necessary Being's reality itself is what makes it true to say that He exists. Nothing is added to Him, and no other aspect is needed—whether a real feature, a relation, or a negation.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00495

Consider the difference between understanding connectedness itself—as when we think of the continuous form of a body—and understanding something, such as matter, that is connected. Likewise, we can understand the Necessary Being as necessity itself, or imagine a thing to which necessity belongs. In the first case, the judgment concerns the thing's own reality and nothing else. In the second, it concerns that reality together with a feature it possesses.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00496

Suppose something called a Necessary Being is not necessary through its own reality. It is then merely a thing described as necessary. Necessity does not belong to it in itself; it appears only when we add a further feature to our account of it. That makes necessity something added, not something essential. And anything that receives such a feature needs a cause other than itself—either a cause that makes it necessary or one that makes the idea of necessity apply to it. For we have already disproved that a thing can cause its own existence and necessity.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00497

So the essence is possible in itself, and its cause makes it necessary. It is therefore not necessary in itself. Every being necessary in itself must be necessity itself, not a thing to which necessity belongs as an inseparable or removable feature. So much for that devilish suggestion.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00498

Many proofs support this central claim in metaphysics. To complete them, we need the premise that God's reality is pure existence, self-subsisting and intensified, and that anything to which existence or necessity belongs as a feature is possible in itself when considered apart from its relation to something else; its existence and necessity come from that other thing. We have already discussed this premise, and it is supported by the arguments in the books of philosophers and mystics. It also clears up the confusion that has troubled many minds in connection with the argument attributed to Ibn Kammūna. Some have called it “the pride of the devils” because it is so difficult to unravel. Yet I have found the same objection in the work of someone who lived before him.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00499

The objection is this: why could there not be two simple realities, whose full natures are unknown and entirely different, each necessary in itself? The concept “necessary in existence” could be drawn from each of them as a feature. They would share this feature, abstracted from their own realities, while differing through their pure, distinct natures.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00500

Here is the answer. Either the concept “necessary in existence” is understood from each thing's own reality, without considering any feature outside it, or it is understood with such a feature in mind. Both possibilities are impossible. The second fails for the reason already given: anything whose reality is not simply the source of existence, necessity, actuality, and completeness is possible in itself and incomplete. The first fails because one concept cannot truly apply to realities that differ in every respect, with no shared feature at all.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00501

In short, a sound and untroubled mind recognises that things which differ simply by being different—with no shared aspect—cannot be the basis or true referent of one and the same judgment. A shared judgment is possible when things agree in the very respect in which we judge them to agree. Zayd and ʿAmr are both human because they share the whole human nature, not because they share their different individual features. A human being and a horse are both animals because they share the broader kind “animal.” Snow and ivory are both white because both have whiteness as a feature. Or they may agree through an external relation: someone might call all categories of possible things “existent” in the derivative sense that they receive existence from the true source—the self-subsisting existence of God, if they think possible things exist only as a mental concept drawn from that relation. Or they may share a negative idea: everything other than the Necessary Being is possible, because its own reality entails neither necessary existence nor necessary nonexistence.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00502

Apart from these ways of agreeing, two things cannot truly share a description unless they share something, either as part of their nature or as an added feature. Now suppose the same judgment applies to realities that differ in their very natures, without our taking any further feature or relation into account. They must share something essential and also differ in something essential. Their reality would therefore have parts: one would be like a broader kind or matter, and the other like a feature that defines the kind or gives matter its form. But whatever has parts cannot be necessary in itself.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00503

More than that, if we reflect on the very concept of existence—the abstract idea we know at once—we are led to understand that the reality it comes from is self-subsisting: the Necessary Truth itself. It is pure existence, free of universality, particularity, multiplicity, and division. If we suppose another thing with this same pure existence, it cannot be distinct from the first. There would not be two; there would be one reality and one existence. As the author of The Book of Flashes says: “Pure existence, beyond which there is nothing fuller: whenever you suppose it a second time and look, it is the same as before, because nothing is distinct from what is pure.” God's necessary existence, which is His very reality, therefore shows that He is one, as the Qur'an says: “God bears witness that there is no god but He.” And it shows that possible things exist through Him, as He says: “Is it not enough that your Lord is witness over all things?”
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00504
A proof from the Throne
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00505

With God's help and the support of His highest realm, we have another proof from the Throne that the Necessary Being is one. It also rules out the possibility just raised. First we must establish a principle.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00506

God's reality is itself what makes it true to say that He exists and is necessary. Nothing apart from His own reality can make this true. If something else had to be considered, He would depend on it for His existence and necessity, as explained earlier. Nor can there be another aspect of His reality that is not existent and necessary. That would make Him composite, either directly or because those aspects depend on further aspects.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00507

God's reality has no parts. He must therefore exist and be necessary in every respect in which anything can truly be said of Him. Suppose He lacked some level of existence, some degree of actuality, or some perfection that belongs to existence as such. In that respect His own reality would fail to be fully existent. Alongside His actuality there would be something merely possible or even impossible. His reality would then have different aspects joined together—in other words, it would be composite. This is what we established in the previous chapter: the Necessary Being must be necessary from every point of view. So every perfection and beauty must belong to God's own reality, even though, in other things, it flows from Him.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00508

Now suppose there were two Necessary Beings. They could not be necessarily connected through their very realities. For such a connection would mean either that one caused the other, or that both depended on a third cause. Either way, something supposed to be necessary in itself would depend on a cause. That contradicts our assumption.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00509

So each of the two would have a level of perfection and a share of existence that the other did not have and that did not flow from the other. Each would lack some level of completeness and existence, whether that level was impossible for it or merely possible. Each one's reality would therefore be the basis both for having one feature and for lacking another. It would not be pure actuality, necessity, and perfection. It would be composite in its very reality, and such composition is incompatible with being necessary in itself.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00510

The Necessary Being must therefore be so complete and fully actual that He includes every level of existence and every perfection that belongs to existence as such. There is nothing equal to Him in existence or excellence. His reality must be the source of all perfections and every good. This proof may not help readers who are still new to philosophy, because it relies on principles established in many different parts of this book. But for someone trained in philosophy, it is stronger than many powerful proofs.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00511
Chapter — Revisiting necessity, possibility, and impossibility, and answering objections about them
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00512

Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī raises an objection about necessity, possibility, and impossibility, the three conditions that enter into our judgments. Suppose necessity necessarily belongs to God's existence. It would then seem to be an effect of that existence. Yet every effect is possible in itself, and whatever is possible becomes necessary through its cause. God's necessity would therefore require a prior necessity, which would require another, without end.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00513

The wise Tusi replies that something can follow necessarily from another thing without being its effect. Necessity, possibility, and impossibility are concepts formed in the mind when we consider things in relation to existence outside it. In that sense, the mind produces the concepts. They are not separate things in the world that cause, or are caused by, the things they describe. For example, thinking about Zayd is caused by the person thinking of him, but it is not a cause of Zayd, nor is it caused by Zayd. For something to be necessary in reality means that when a thinker considers it as related to real existence, the idea of necessity follows in the mind.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00514

Another objection: necessity and its opposite, non-necessity, are contradictories. Non-necessity is nothing, so necessity must be something real. And necessity is the strengthening of existence—how, then, could it be unreal?
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00515

The answer is that “unreal” here does not mean absolute nonexistence, or an idea whose very meaning is that something is denied. It means something that does not exist in the external world but does exist in the mind. Contradictory ideas divide every concept between them, but that does not mean that each must exist outside the mind. Is “impossible” not the opposite of “possible in the broad sense”? Yet impossible things do not exist in the world; and not every broadly possible thing has to exist there either.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00516

A further objection concerns what it means for a feature to belong to something. We do not need to say that the feature exists independently in the same place as its subject. We need only say that the subject has it. So we can attribute even a concept such as blindness to something outside the mind. But it is a familiar principle that a feature's existence in itself is the same as its existence in its subject. Therefore, mental features such as these would have to exist in the external world as accidents in things. The mind rejects the idea that concepts like these are external realities, much less accidents in the world.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00517

The answer depends on the two meanings of existence in relation to something else. One is the link between a subject and what we say of it in a statement. The other is the way a quality or form exists in the thing that bears it. These are not the same. A quality such as whiteness can exist in its own right as a quality and can also be attributed to a body. Blindness, by contrast, need not have an existence of its own in order to be truly attributed to someone. Confuse these two kinds of connection, and the objection will seem to follow, even though it does not.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00518

Another objection follows. If possibility has no reality of its own outside the mind, then, the objection says, things are possible only in our thoughts. But anything outside the mind must fall into one of the three alternatives: necessary, possible, or impossible. If the middle alternative is excluded, only necessity and impossibility remain. That cannot be right.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00519

The answer is already before us. A statement can be true of something outside the mind without the concept used to describe it existing there as a separate thing. The same applies to impossibility: it has no form of its own in the external world, yet things can truly be called impossible. This resolves the objection.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00520

It also resolves an apparent dispute among philosophers. Aristotle's followers say that general concepts such as necessity, possibility, causation, and priority exist outside the mind. Earlier philosophers of the Portico say that these concepts exist only when the mind considers them. Look closely, however, and the two positions need not conflict. The earlier philosophers deny that these concepts exist in their own right. Aristotle's followers affirm that they can truly be said of things outside the mind. They are speaking of different ways of existing.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00521

You can now see the weakness of an argument found in some works of theology. It treats the alleged lack of difference between denying possibility and denying a possibility as proof that possibility must be something real. It also argues that every absence is understood through existence, and therefore that whatever has an absence must have some positive reality. If they mean that possibility exists in the world as a separate thing, they are plainly wrong. If they mean that it is not sheer nothingness but a concept that the mind can truly apply to things, whether they are thought of or exist outside it, that is exactly what the philosophers maintain. “Its possibility is denied” does not mean that the idea of possibility has external existence; “it is not possible” means that the predicate “possible” does not apply, as with other mental concepts used to describe things.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00522

Nor must every negation be defined by reference to existence. Nonexistence itself is the denial of existence. But other negations need not be: possibility, for example, denies necessity; and we can also deny a denial. If by ‘existence’ we mean simply something affirmed in relation to something else, then every denial does presuppose an affirmation in that limited sense. What is denied is not itself the denial of its denial; in that respect it has a kind of relative affirmation. That is what matters when we define an unqualified kind of negation. As Avicenna says in The Healing, unqualified affirmation is broader than something's existing as a reality in itself; it can also mean that something exists only in relation to another. Such an affirmation can be part of how we explain a negation, without being something that exists inside the negation. Some commentators on Aristotle have mistaken an element of the explanation for something that exists within the negation itself. But what is denied cannot exist together with its own denial. When people say that sight is part of the definition of blindness, they do not mean that a blind person has sight. They mean only that blindness cannot be explained without referring to sight. A definition can say more than the thing it defines.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00523

Another objection: treating possibility and the other general concepts as mental ideas may stop an infinite regress in the external world, but it does not stop one in the mind when it considers things one by one. If something is possible, that possibility must apply to it necessarily; otherwise it could change from possible to not possible. So the possibility of the thing must itself be necessary in the mind, and the mind's recognition of that necessity must also be necessary, and so on without end. In any case, if a thing is possible, the mind must necessarily describe it as possible.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00524

The answer is that the chain here has no fixed end only because the mind keeps working through it. The argument itself does not compel us to continue forever; the chain stops when the mind stops considering it.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00525

Here is the point in more detail. There is a difference between something being an object the mind examines and its being a tool the mind uses to understand something else. When we understand a human being through the idea of a human, the idea is our tool; we are not looking at the idea itself. We do not judge that this idea is a substance or an accident when we judge that a human being is an animal and a substance. If we turn our attention to the idea in the mind and examine it as an object, then we find that it is an accident existing in something else.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00526

When careful philosophers say that the form present in the mind is what we know directly, they mean that it does not need another form to make it known. They do not mean that, when we understand what a human being is and judge that a human is a bodily animal and a substance, the object of our thought is the mental image itself—one of the qualities of the soul. That would plainly be wrong.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00527

Necessity, possibility, and impossibility work in much the same way. We use them to consider whether, and how, a thing exists. While we are using them to understand that thing, we are not asking whether these concepts themselves exist or whether they themselves are necessary, possible, or impossible. If the mind turns to one of these ideas and makes it an object of thought, then it is no longer possibility, necessity, or impossibility as a tool for understanding something else. It is now an idea in the mind, an accident existing in a subject, and is itself possible in relation to its own existence.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00528

The same holds for words and concepts that serve only to connect things. When the mind stops using them as links and begins to consider them directly, they become concepts in their own right, like nouns. There is nothing impossible about that change. Think of matter becoming formed, of a general kind becoming more specific through what distinguishes it, of what is possible becoming actual, or of what is incomplete reaching completion. It is not like one fully formed thing changing into another fully formed thing. A connecting word, while it serves as a connection, is not a complete thing in itself. It is a relation between things. And a thing is not the same as its relation, any more than something actual is the same as the mere capacity to become actual.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00529

What you may have heard—that relational existence and independent existence are entirely different in reality—means what we have just explained. It does not mean that there are two separate realities of existence. A relation has no complete reality of its own, just as a mirror has no color of its own. It receives colors and shows other realities. The difference is in the concept and the way the mind considers it, not in two complete realities that differ in their own nature. It is like the difference between something complete and something not yet complete but capable of becoming so, or between a thing and what is not yet a thing but can become one.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00530

Once you have understood why this chain of thoughts ends when the mind stops considering it, the same principle can guide you elsewhere. It applies to other general ideas that can be repeated without end—unity, existence, necessity, and the like—whether or not they correspond to something outside the mind. Existence and unity are realities in the world, yet their concepts can recur in the mind without end: existence itself exists, and the existence of existence can in turn be considered as existing, and so on until the mind stops. The one reality that makes all these endlessly repeated judgments true is existence itself, which exists in its own right. The same is true of unity.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00531

Someone may press the objection further. The mind can recognise necessary connections without end. If any link were allowed to fail, the connection with which we started would no longer be necessary. It seems, then, that we must affirm the necessity of every link in the endless chain. Yet a true affirmative statement needs a subject that exists. Does that not mean that all these links must themselves exist?
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00532

Have you forgotten what we explained and what your insight had already reached, so that you would not misuse your reasoning? A connection is a connection only when the mind considers it as a link, not as a concept in its own right. As a link, it is not a thing to which the mind can apply “necessary” or “not necessary.” If the mind turns its attention to it and examines it as a concept or feature, then it can ask whether it is necessary. But the subject of the judgment that a link cannot be broken is the link the mind has noticed and examined as an object—not the link simply in its role as a relation. There is no need for every link to be examined in this way. The mind's sequence of thoughts comes to an end at some point.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00533

This is a better answer than the one offered by the author of The Commentary on the Abstract to untie the knot. He says that such necessary connections exist in reality through the things they are drawn from, not as distinct mental forms. A true affirmative judgment requires its subject to exist, but that existence can take forms other than a distinct individual thing. For example, we may truthfully say that one part of a continuous body is hot and another cold, even before the body has been physically divided.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00534

An external statement may require its subject to exist outside the mind in a particular way. A judgment that something occupies space requires an independently existing thing; a judgment about the properties of a substance requires existence in the way appropriate to substance. In the same way, particular kinds of mental judgment require particular ways for their subjects to exist in the mind.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00535

Some necessary connections depend on both the thing and what follows from it existing in reality. In other cases, one side exists in reality, while the other need only be something that can rightly be drawn from it. For example, the finite limit of a body is a negative feature that necessarily follows from its being finite. A connection can also depend on the potential for a concept to be drawn from something, without that concept yet being drawn. That is how one connection may necessarily follow from another: it is enough that the second can be drawn from what exists. The comparison ends with this claim: just as a statement of possibility need only allow its subject to exist, a judgment about a necessary connection need only allow that connection to be drawn from something that actually exists.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00536

For all his care, this does not resolve the difficulty. So long as a connection remains something that could be drawn from a thing, but has not actually been considered, it cannot itself be the subject of a true judgment about necessity. It is still only a connection, not yet a concept the mind has taken up for examination. If the mind does consider it directly and judges whether it is necessary, the connection has become a concept actually present to the mind. It now has mental existence in its own right. In that respect it is not simply an attribute that exists only through the thing from which it was drawn.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00537

Nor can the existence of a thing be exactly the same as the existence of an attribute, whether the attribute is part of the thing in reality or something understood by the mind. Otherwise we could no longer distinguish what belongs to a thing in itself from what is attributed to it. For example, the heavens exist as heavens; their being above something is not simply their existence as heavens.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00538

The heavens exist in their own right. To say that they are above something, however, is to describe a relation. That relation is not simply the heavens' own existence. Necessity is similar. When one thing necessarily follows from another, the connection can be real, and if it holds between things outside the mind, we can call it a connection in the world. But the connection does not exist in the independent way that either of the things does. Only when we consider it directly does it become an object of thought.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00539

Negations and absences show the same distinction. When the mind considers them, they acquire a kind of mental existence, yet they remain negations and absences in what they mean. The reach of existence, as understood by the mind, extends even to the concept of nonexistence, a supposed partner of God, and the impossible joining of contradictions. A relation, likewise, is relational in what it means, even when we consider it as something present to our thought. Keep that distinction in view.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00540

I also find several further problems with his account. First, we cannot make true external judgments about parts of a continuous whole before it has been divided into distinct parts—unless two different, stable qualities have already divided it in some way. Once there is an actual division, each part exists separately in the world. Before that, neither part exists on its own; only the matter that can be divided is there. Besides, on this view, existence itself is only a mental relation drawn from something else. It is one when its source is one and many when its source is many. How, then, can many different things exist through one existence?
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00541

Second, different judgments may demand different kinds of existence from their subjects. But the bare possibility of drawing a concept from something is not enough. The subject must exist in the way that the judgment requires. Before the mind has actually considered a connection, that connection is still only something it could use to understand another thing. It is not yet an independent subject of judgment.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00542

Third, a possible judgment does not require its subject to exist independently in the outside world, but it does require the subject to exist in the mind, at least in a general, undivided way. These judgments require their subjects' presence even more strongly than possible judgments do. How, then, could a merely potential, relational existence be enough for their subjects?
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00543

Fourth, consider the claim that a statement of possibility does not require its subject to exist in the world. That does not mean we can truly say, while Zayd does not exist, that he may be a writer. In this argument, Zayd's possibility of writing concerns his condition in the world; such a condition cannot belong to him there unless he exists. The point is that the possible connection between subject and predicate does not, by itself, require the subject to exist. Other aspects of the statement may require this: the statement as a whole may be about something in the world, apart from its modality. A modality that does not require the subject's existence does not prevent the judgment itself from requiring it. The discussion is about the judgments, not only about their modalities; and in the case before us, the modality is necessity.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00544
Chapter — Different meanings of “possible”
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00545

In ordinary speech, we call something possible when its existence is not impossible. We also use the word when a relation stated between two things is not impossible. Here impossible means either that a thing must fail to exist or that a stated relation must fail to hold. So, in both uses, possible means that the opposite is not necessary. Strictly, this absence of necessity belongs to the opposite side of the statement. Applying it to the relation we are discussing is a figure of speech: we describe one side by reference to the other.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00546

In this first usage, what is not possible is impossible, while what is possible includes both what is necessary and what is neither necessary nor impossible. The term does not include the impossible that it opposes. Nor does this usage name an actual shared kind that exists in its own right. In reality, something is either necessary or possible; the mind alone forms the general concept that covers both. There is no separate, unfinished nature in the world that contains them both. That is why this general possibility is a modality—a way of describing a statement—not a material part of what exists.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00547

A later use broadened the direction in which the word could be applied. Since impossibility may concern either an affirmation or a denial, people began denying necessity on either side. Taken in one direction, this sense of possibility can include what is impossible; taken in the other, it includes what is neither necessary nor impossible. It excludes what is necessary. A more precise use then emerged: possibility in the strict sense means that neither affirmation nor denial is necessary. It is opposed to necessity on both sides and is narrower than the first, general meaning.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00548

A third meaning of possible rules out every kind of necessity: necessity in itself, through a particular description, or at a particular time. This comes closer than either earlier meaning to a true middle ground between affirmation and denial. For that reason, it has the strongest claim to the name possibility. Take a human being’s ability to write. Human nature is equally related to having this ability and not having it. A statement may still be necessary once its subject has the predicate: writing is necessary insofar as it exists. But the same case can be described as possible when we consider what writing is in itself. This meaning is narrower than the two earlier meanings only by analogy, not in the strict sense.
